# Week 50 Appendix: A Week Measured by What Held

*Immigration enforcement widened, vetoes punished disfavored places, and a cultural institution changed its own rules — while courts and one peaceful inauguration held the line.*

![Header image](image_wide_week50_appendix.png)

This was a high-pressure week defined less by a single constitutional rupture than by a broad pattern of executive aggrandizement, coercive immigration governance, retaliatory use of state power, and symbolic capture of public institutions. The strongest pressures fell on traits involving rule by executive fiat, stratified citizenship, weaponized law, politicized civil service, and federal punishment of disfavored communities or jurisdictions. Immigration was the clearest structural arena: denaturalization quotas, paused proceedings for nationals of 19 countries, aggressive street and courthouse enforcement, and a major ICE recruitment expansion all pushed toward a system where legal status is contingent and coercive. At the same time, Trump-linked vetoes of bipartisan water and Everglades measures suggested retaliation as a governing method, while the Kennedy Center bylaw change showed how institutional rules can be rewritten to convert public bodies into instruments of personal glorification. Courts provided some countervailing repair, especially in the CFPB funding order and the dismissal of charges in an ICE-related case, but those checks were partial and reactive rather than system-setting.

Power and Authority

1. Donald Trump urged Senate Republicans to eliminate the filibuster (2025-12-27): The push targeted a key minority check in the Senate and would have made it easier for a governing majority to pass laws without cross-party restraint.

2. Federal agents deployed in military fatigues in major cities (2025-12-27) *[single source]*: The use of heavily armed federal personnel in civilian spaces signaled a more coercive federal posture toward protest and local unrest.

3. The U.S. military conducted strikes in Nigeria and Syria (2025-12-28): The strikes extended executive use of force abroad and raised oversight questions about how military action was framed and authorized.

4. USCIS issued guidance seeking 100 to 200 denaturalization case referrals per month (2025-12-30): The guidance expanded the state's capacity to strip citizenship, increasing insecurity for naturalized Americans and widening executive leverage over legal status.

5. USCIS paused immigration proceedings for nationals of 19 countries (2025-12-30) *[single source]*: The pause blocked paths to citizenship and residency for targeted nationalities, concentrating executive control over who could complete lawful status processes.

6. ICE announced a $100 million recruitment campaign for new agents (2025-12-31): The campaign aimed to rapidly expand deportation capacity, deepening the federal government's coercive reach in immigration enforcement.

7. The Kennedy Center board changed its bylaws to limit voting to Trump-appointed trustees (2025-12-31): The bylaw change narrowed outside oversight and concentrated control of a public cultural institution in a politically aligned bloc.

8. Donald Trump ended efforts to deploy National Guard troops in Democratic-led cities (2025-12-31) *[single source]*: The reversal followed court setbacks and highlighted how federal troop deployment had been used as leverage against disfavored local governments.

9. Donald Trump vetoed an Everglades project bill affecting the Miccosukee Tribe (2026-01-01) *[single source]*: The veto withheld federal support from a tribal and environmental project, showing executive power used in a way that burdened a disfavored community.

10. Donald Trump vetoed a bipartisan Colorado drinking water bill (2026-01-01): The veto blocked a unanimously passed public works measure and raised concerns that federal power was being used to punish political opponents.

11. President Trump issued an executive order blocking HieFo Corporation from acquiring Emcore assets (2026-01-02): The order showed direct presidential intervention in a private transaction on national security grounds, reinforcing broad executive control over strategic assets.

12. The White House asserted personal control over immigration policy, criminal law, and renditions (2026-01-02) *[single source]*: The reported posture blurred legal and institutional limits by concentrating coercive state functions in the presidency.

2. The House of Representatives passed a resolution condemning Chuy Garcia's alleged election manipulation (2025-12-27): The resolution addressed a lawmaker's conduct tied to succession and electoral fairness, using House procedure to police representation norms.
